subject: David's census of Israel and Judah, plague casualties, and price of Ornan's threshing floor

figures.name: Israel's fighting men (sword-drawing)
figures.note: MT and LXX agree at 1,100,000; SP does not contain Chronicles.

figures.name: Judah's fighting men (sword-drawing)
figures.note: LXX reads 480,000 against MT's 470,000; 2 Samuel 24:9 MT gives 500,000 for Judah, showing inter-textual variation.

figures.name: Plague casualties
figures.note: Agreement across MT and LXX, also matching 2 Samuel 24:15.

figures.name: Price of threshing floor (shekels of gold)
figures.note: MT and LXX agree at 600 shekels of gold by weight, contrasting with 2 Samuel 24:24's 50 shekels of silver.

figures.name: Years of famine offered as judgment
figures.note: MT and LXX agree on 3 years; 2 Samuel 24:13 MT reads 7, LXX Samuel reads 3, a famous synoptic divergence.

systematic_analysis.pattern: The divergences within 1 Chronicles 21 between MT and LXX are minimal—essentially limited to Judah's muster (470,000 vs 480,000)—and SP is irrelevant since the Samaritan canon excludes Chronicles. The more significant numerical tensions lie in the synoptic comparison with 2 Samuel 24 (Israel 800,000 vs 1,100,000; Judah 500,000 vs 470,000/480,000; 7 vs 3 years of famine; 50 silver shekels vs 600 gold shekels), which reflect either independent source traditions or theological/scribal harmonization rather than a systematic mathematical rule.
systematic_analysis.pattern_plain: Within Chronicles itself the Greek and Hebrew versions barely differ. The bigger puzzle is that Chronicles reports very different numbers than the parallel account in 2 Samuel 24.

theories.name: Independent Source Traditions
theories.summary: The Chronicler likely drew on a Vorlage of Samuel distinct from proto-MT Samuel, possibly closer to 4QSam-a or LXX Samuel, accounting for the divergent census totals and famine duration. The internal MT/LXX agreement in Chronicles suggests stable transmission of the Chronicler's source, while the disagreement with Samuel reflects pre-existing variation in the Davidic narrative tradition.
theories.summary_plain: The author of Chronicles probably used a different version of Samuel than the one we have today, which explains why his numbers differ. Once Chronicles was written, its numbers were copied faithfully.
supporting_evidence: 4QSamuel-a preserves readings closer to Chronicles than to MT Samuel in several places, demonstrating textual plurality.
LXX Samuel reads 3 years of famine against MT Samuel's 7, agreeing with Chronicles and showing pre-Christian variation.
MT and LXX Chronicles agree on nearly all figures, suggesting a stable Chronicler tradition.
The Chronicler's gold/silver price difference (600 vs 50) may reflect a distinct cultic-theological source emphasizing the temple site's value.
weaknesses: Cannot fully explain the Judah figure variation (470,000 vs 480,000) within Chronicles itself.
Some divergences may still reflect deliberate theological reshaping by the Chronicler rather than Vorlage difference.
Lacks Qumran evidence specifically for Chronicles to confirm Vorlage hypotheses.

theories.name: Scribal Error in Numerical Transmission
theories.summary: Hebrew numerical notation using letters or abbreviated forms is notoriously vulnerable to corruption, and the 470,000/480,000 LXX-MT split for Judah likely reflects confusion of similar numerical signs. Larger Samuel/Chronicles divergences may compound original scribal slips with later harmonization attempts.
theories.summary_plain: Numbers were easy to miscopy in Hebrew, and small errors in one tradition were not corrected in the other. This explains minor differences like 470,000 versus 480,000.
supporting_evidence: The 10,000 difference in Judah's census fits common confusion patterns in Hebrew numeral letters.
Number variations between MT and LXX appear sporadically across Chronicles without theological motive.
Ancient Hebrew numerical abbreviations are attested in epigraphy and prone to misreading.
Round numbers (70,000; 600; 1,100,000) transmit stably while precise figures vary.
weaknesses: Cannot account for the magnitude of the Samuel/Chronicles divergence in Israel's total (300,000 difference).
The price change from silver to gold is qualitative, not a simple numerical slip.
Pure scribal error cannot explain the 7→3 years of famine variant.

theories.name: Theological Motivation
theories.summary: The Chronicler systematically magnifies figures associated with the temple site and David's preparations: 600 gold shekels for the future temple location versus 50 silver shekels in Samuel, and inflated military totals reinforcing Israel's grandeur. Satan's introduction as inciter (1 Chr 21:1) likewise shows theological reshaping, suggesting numbers participate in the Chronicler's program.
theories.summary_plain: The author of Chronicles may have changed numbers on purpose to highlight the importance of the temple and David's kingdom. The high price for the threshing floor signals that this is the future temple site.
supporting_evidence: 600 gold shekels vastly exceeds 50 silver shekels, fitting Chronicles' temple-glorification agenda.
Chronicles consistently inflates figures elsewhere (e.g., 1 Chr 19:18 vs 2 Sam 10:18).
The shift from 7 to 3 years balances the threefold options offered to David (symmetry-driven).
Satan replacing YHWH as inciter shows the Chronicler willingly reshapes the narrative theologically.
weaknesses: Does not explain the minor MT/LXX split within Chronicles itself.
Some 'inflations' may simply reflect a different Vorlage rather than the Chronicler's own editing.
Theological motive is harder to demonstrate than to assert for specific numbers.

overall_assessment: 1 Chronicles 21 shows remarkable internal stability between MT and LXX, with only the Judah muster (470,000/480,000) diverging meaningfully; the Samaritan Pentateuch is not a witness here. The principal text-critical interest lies in the synoptic divergences from 2 Samuel 24, best explained by a combination of independent source traditions (the Chronicler's Vorlage of Samuel differed from proto-MT Samuel, as Qumran and LXX Samuel evidence suggests) and deliberate theological reshaping (especially the 600-gold-shekel price elevating the temple site). Minor MT/LXX variation within Chronicles is best attributed to ordinary scribal transmission of numerals. The passage illustrates that even when Greek and Hebrew Chronicles agree, the deeper textual history of the Hebrew Bible was pluriform well into the Second Temple period.
overall_plain: The Greek and Hebrew versions of 1 Chronicles 21 agree almost completely, but they both differ sharply from the parallel story in 2 Samuel 24. The likeliest explanation is that the Chronicler used a different version of Samuel than ours and also reshaped some details to emphasize the temple's importance.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Synoptic divergence outweighs intra-Chronicles textual variation
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most striking finding is that the real numerical problem is not MT-versus-LXX within Chronicles but Chronicles-versus-Samuel, pointing to textual pluriformity in the Davidic narrative tradition before canonical fixation. This implies that any 'original' biblical chronology of David's census is methodologically unrecoverable without reckoning with multiple Hebrew editions of Samuel circulating in the Second Temple period. The 600-gold-shekel price further suggests theology and transmission are entangled, not separable.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The big lesson is that the Bible's own parallel accounts disagree more than the Greek and Hebrew manuscripts of Chronicles do. This shows the text was still being shaped and reshaped well into ancient Jewish history.
